claims.text: A disorder-to-order phase transition induced by thermal treatment can overcome structural or chemical instability in crystalline, near-equiatomic nanoparticles containing five or more metals.
The proposed intervention is a single, unique thermal treatment that induces a disorder-to-order phase transition.
The thermal treatment produces an ordered phase structure in the nanoparticles.
The disorder-to-order transition is driven by thermodynamic stability.
A thermodynamic preference for a stable single phase can be associated with resistance to phase separation in quinary high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
The ordered phase prevents phase separation or chemical instability.
The intervention is applicable throughout the 773–1173 K catalytic regime.
Thermally treated, ordered nanoparticles will have better thermal stability than the same nanoparticles without the disorder-to-order transition.
Thermally treated, ordered nanoparticles will have better chemical stability than the same nanoparticles without the disorder-to-order transition.
The intervention may enhance catalytic performance relative to nanoparticles without the transition.
The compositional boundary is nanoparticles containing five or more metals.
XRD, TEM, and XPS can be used during or after thermal exposure to characterize nanoparticle structure and composition.
Observation of significant phase separation or chemical instability during thermal exposure would falsify the hypothesis.
